title: The cabin's cost
hookLine: he lists every expense of his cabin: 28 dollars and twelve and a half cents (Walden 1)

cards: Boards. Old bricks. Two secondhand windows.
Nails, hinges and screws, a latch, a little chalk. In the middle of Walden, a book full of pond water and birdsong, Thoreau stops and prints a receipt.

Line by line, he lists what his cabin cost him, then adds it up, down to the half cent: twenty-eight dollars and twelve and a half cents. It's an odd page to find among the pond water. It's also a candid one.

teach.b: You met his idea of cost back on day nine hundred three; here's the receipt behind it. First, a borrowed axe. Thoreau began by borrowing one, and he gave it back sharper than he got it.
Second, the list. He builds mostly from used materials: boards from an old shanty, secondhand bricks and windows. He isn't embarrassed by how small the numbers are.
He's proud of them. The chapter is called Economy, and he means it literally. Third, the real price.

Here's the sentence that turns the receipt into philosophy: "the cost of a thing is the amount of what I will call life which is required to be exchanged for it, immediately or in the long run." Not dollars. Life.
Hours of work, years of payments, the evenings spent earning what a thing requires. By that measure, a bigger house can be very expensive indeed, even if the bank approves it. Fourth, why it matters.
Thoreau isn't saying everyone should live in a cabin.
He's asking his readers to write their own receipt.
A price tag says what a thing costs in money, and nothing about what it costs in life.
This week ran from Emerson's long goodbye to Thoreau's workbench, his grief for John, the river trip, then Walden's warnings about quiet desperation and new clothes.
The last of those days circle one plain question, and the receipt puts it in ink: what is a life being exchanged for, and is it worth it?

how: Some readers of Walden keep a simple record of what they spend, in money and in time, after Thoreau's own itemized account of building his cabin.

games.q: you need an axe to start building, and you don't own one. what does Thoreau do?
o: buy the best axe in town.
borrow one, and give it back sharper.
wait until he can afford one.
games.why: he borrowed an axe, and says he returned it sharper than he received it. the cabin begins with a loan, returned improved.

practice: In your mind, start a short list, not of what you want but of what you actually need to live well this week: a place to sleep, food, a few people, some quiet.
Then notice one thing that isn't on the list, something that's been costing you a lot of life lately, in hours or in worry. Just notice it, with no verdict.
